entry.title: Agent memory needs its OpenTelemetry moment
entry.content:
Every agent tool stores memory in its own shape, and every week someone builds another one. None of them can read the others. Observability had the same problem until OpenTelemetry gave everyone one data model to share. A tour of today's memory formats, the proposals that already exist, and what a shared spec could look like.

List every place your coding tools keep something they "remember". A typical setup today:

an AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md in most repos, and .cursor/rules/*.mdc in a few

an agent writing files to a /memories directory through Anthropic's memory tool

Copilot keeping facts about each repo on GitHub's side

a memory MCP server keeping a JSONL knowledge graph

That's four different shapes, and none of them can read the others. A lesson your CI agent learns stays in whatever wrote it. Your editor agent can't read it, and neither can the next tool you try.

Each format is reasonable on its own. Together, they rebuild the same small idea again and again: a note an agent left for its future self, stored at some address, true for a while.

And the list keeps growing. Browse r/ClaudeAI, r/LocalLLaMA or r/cursor and you'll find a steady stream of "I built a memory layer for my agent" posts, each with its own storage, its own schema and its own MCP tools. That's good evidence the problem is real: people keep hitting it badly enough to build something. But every new solution adds one more format that nothing else can read. The problem isn't a missing tool. It's a missing agreement, and that only comes from the community working on it together.

I build one of these tools, LoreKit, which is open source. This isn't a pitch that LoreKit has solved memory. Its format is one proposal among several, with gaps of its own. The point is that this is the moment to agree on a shared shape, and that another field has already shown how.

Before 2019, every observability vendor shipped its own agent, its own instrumentation library and its own data format. Switching vendors meant instrumenting your code again. Two open projects, OpenTracing and OpenCensus, tried to fix that and competed with each other too.

In 2019 they merged into OpenTelemetry. What mattered was what the vendors agreed to stop competing on:

A data model: what a span, a metric and a log record are.

Semantic conventions: shared names like service.name and http.*.

A protocol: OTLP, one way to send the data.

Reference implementations: shared SDKs and the Collector.

Vendors kept competing on what they do with the data: storage, querying, analysis. Users instrument once. I work with OpenTelemetry every day at Dash0, and that agreement is why a whole ecosystem of tools can read each other's data.

Agent memory is where observability was before 2019. The timing is good: the formats are young enough to change, and there's already a neutral home for agent standards. MCP and AGENTS.md both sit under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation.

These change quickly, so treat the details as a snapshot from late 2026.

A few of them got something right that a shared spec should keep. Copilot Memory pairs citations you can check against the code with forgetting by default, though it's locked inside one product. LangGraph shows how small the core can be: put(namespace, key, value). Graphiti models time properly, with separate timelines for when a fact was true and when it was recorded. And AGENTS.md shows that a plain file at a known path can become a standard.

Several people have started on this. MacPaw Research's Portable Memory is a .mem bundle with byte-reproducible serialization, deletion tombstones and optional signing; its authors say it isn't widely adopted yet. The Open Memory Protocol is an April 2026 draft for moving conversations and the memories derived from them between platforms as a ZIP with a manifest. Cognee's COGX format imports from Mem0, Letta and Zep.

These mostly solve export: moving one person's memory from vendor A to vendor B. Coding tools also have a second, open problem: live addressing. When a CI job, an editor agent and a review bot work in the same repo at once, how do they read and write the same place and agree on what it means? A complete spec needs both.

Strip away the branding and every format answers the same four questions differently: where a memory is true, what its identity is (does a second write update it or duplicate it?), what it says, and when it stops being true. Nobody disagrees that those matter. The tools only disagree on the answers, which is where OpenTelemetry started too.

There's one real fork: who writes the memory. In instruction files it's a person. In the memory tool, Letta and LoreKit, it's the model. In Mem0 and Graphiti, a service extracts facts from the conversation. A spec doesn't need to pick one. It needs to record which, so a reader knows how much to trust what it reads.

Here's roughly what one record could look like as a file. It illustrates the data model; the field names aren't a proposal:

---spec: agent-memory/0.1id: 8f0c2a6e-4b1d-4c7a-9e2f-3a5b6c7d8e9faddress: { level: repo, value: github.com/acme/checkout }key: tests-need-local-postgreskind: lessonwritten_by: { type: agent, name: claude-code }content_type: text/markdownlifecycle: { expires_at: null, extended_by: write }attributes: { vcs.pr: 482, ci.run_url: "https://ci.example/runs/123" }---Integration tests fail with `ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:5432` unless Postgresis already running. Start it before `pnpm test`: docker compose up -d dbThe test setup does not start it for you.

The frontmatter is the envelope: address and key say where it's true, id is its identity, lifecycle says when it stops, and written_by answers the fork. The Markdown below it is the memory itself, and content_type tells a reader how to treat it. Anything else a tool needs goes in attributes, under a namespace other tools can ignore. The same record serialises to JSON just as well, for a tool that wants to send it over the wire.

Around that record, a spec would mirror OpenTelemetry's layers:

Conventions: shared names for address levels (global, project, repo, branch, and whatever monorepos need), for kinds, and for attribute namespaces (vcs.*, ci.*, agent.*), in one versioned registry.

A contract: a few operations (write, read, list, search, archive) with fixed inputs and outputs, exposed over MCP. Many memory servers now offer an MCP interface, but each exposes different tools with different meanings.

Conformance tests in place of a reference implementation: round-trip a record and check nothing was lost, check that unknown attributes survive a rewrite, check that expiry behaves as stated.

What stays out matters as much: storage, ranking, embeddings, the user interface. That's where tools should compete. And the spec should live somewhere neutral, not in LoreKit's repo or any single vendor's.

"You build a memory tool, so of course you want a standard shaped like it." Fair. It's why LoreKit is one row in the table rather than the template. If a shared spec looks different, LoreKit should adopt it anyway.

"MCP already is the standard." MCP standardises the call, not the record. OpenTelemetry needed a protocol and a data model. Memory needs both too.

"Shared memory is a prompt-injection channel." Yes. Anything an agent reads can steer it, and shared memory widens who gets to write it. A spec should make that visible: record who wrote each memory, allow signatures (Portable Memory already does), and let a record point at the code it depends on so a reader can check whether that code changed. No format makes poisoning impossible.

"Another standard won't fix fragmentation." That's xkcd 927, and it's the strongest objection. My answer is OpenTelemetry's: agreement came when existing projects merged, not when someone added another one. The work here is the same: take what the existing proposals and tools each got right, and agree on the parts they share.

I don't know the answers to these, and I'd rather work them out in public:

Which address levels? Monorepos want a level between repo and branch. Should levels be a fixed list or conventions?

Should forgetting be the default? Copilot forgets by default, LoreKit doesn't, and LangGraph extends life on read.

Should a record point at the code it depends on? It's the best protection against stale memory, but it ties a record to a code host.

Who should coordinate? A working group, a foundation, or a draft spec people send changes to?

If you build any of the tools in the table, or wrote one of the proposals, I'd like to compare notes. LoreKit's schema and on-disk format are MIT-licensed as one concrete input. To see real records, LoreKit's offline store writes plain Markdown files you can open, grep and diff:

npx @lorekit/cli install

Compare them with what your other tools write, and tell me what a shared format would need that none of them have yet.

llama-modchip is a set of ggml/llama.cpp kernel patches, quantization transcoders, and runtime tools designed to run sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) checkpoints entirely in system RAM on x86_64 (AVX-512 / AVX2) and ARM64 (NEON / SVE / Apple Metal) processors:

Fitting 284B DeepSeek-V4-Flash into 64 GB Physical RAM (56.56 GiB on disk, 1.71 bpw): Standard UD-IQ1_S builds of DeepSeek-V4-Flash (284.33B total, 13.17B active across 43 MLA layers and 256 routed experts) occupy 76.87 GiB (82.5 GB), exceeding the ~62.5 GiB of usable RAM on a 64 GB Linux system and causing page-cache thrashing or OOM kills. llama-modchip reduces the checkpoint to 56.56 GiB (60.73 GB) so the entire model plus a 256K KV cache (57.61–58.9 GiB VmRSS) locks into RAM with zero swap. By default, all 6 routed experts per layer (Top-6) are evaluated without pruning. CPU Cache & SIMD Kernel Patches (+77% prefill, +53% decode): Replaces single-column quantized matrix-vector loops during prompt prefill with a 4-level register (ZMM AVX-512BW) + L1D (32 KB) + L2 (1 MB) + L3 (64 MB) multi-column ({8,4,3,2}) tiling schedule (25.0 -> 44.36 tok/s on 16-core Zen 5), register-stationary MQA8 FlashAttention, and non-temporal _MM_HINT_NTA MoE streaming so cold expert weights do not evict hot KV cache lines from L3. Self-Speculative Drafting & Instant Agent Context Restore: Pairs a 1.64 MB L2/L3 Zobrist n-gram drafter (Stockfish-PVS v2) with /dev/shm KV slot snapshots (13.1–32.6 ms restore time for 40-tool Claude Code prompts) and an $O(1)$speculative rollback fix fordeepseek4 recurrent/MLA states.

entry.title: Writing as a thinking tool
entry.content:
Writing as a thinking tool

In middle school I could not get through long passages no matter how hard I tried. I would read an entire page and find that nothing had registered, so I started taking notes out of desperation. This was the late 80s, and Tony Buzan's mind maps had just reached Turkey. This led me to produce pages and pages of notes that looked like spiderwebs. Creating those notes have helped me tremendously. I made sense of what I was reading by figuring out which branch they would hang off in my mind maps. I realized my pages were not for storing the information as much as they were for processing it.

It took me another ten years to understand why this works so well. During a stretch of PhD procrastination, I read Manuel Blum's advice to graduate students:

You are all computer scientists.

You know what FINITE AUTOMATA can do.

You know what TURING MACHINES can do.

For example, Finite Automata can add but not multiply.

Turing Machines can compute any computable function.

Turing machines are incredibly more powerful than Finite Automata.

Yet the only difference between a FA and a TM is that

the TM, unlike the FA, has paper and pencil.

Think about it.

It tells you something about the power of writing.

Without writing, you are reduced to a finite automaton.

With writing you have the extraordinary power of a Turing machine.

This is a crisp technical claim about which problems you can solve with writing. If you take the paper away, you downgrade yourself by an entire complexity class!

I think this explains a lot about human history as well. Language let us externalize some of our thinking, and our species got smarter. Writing let us externalize even more of it, and we got smarter again. I suspect this is also why LLMs are as capable as they are: so much of our intelligence is already deposited in language that a model trained on it inherits a good deal of intelligence for free.

Out-of-core execution

When we write, we are externalizing our thinking onto paper, and that is what raises our capability to think bigger thoughts. I liken this to out-of-core execution, or external memory algorithms.

A good example of this for me is reviewing a paper. When I read a paper, I think I understand it, and then I sit down to write the review and find out I understood maybe 60% of it. While writing the review, I end up contextualizing the paper better, and get to understand it fully. And sometimes I even realize the ideas are bigger than the authors noticed, and they connect to many other things.

Sometimes the unearthing goes further than understanding one paper. In 2018, I wrote a quick post about the anatomical similarities between Paxos and Nakamoto consensus. I had not started with that thesis originally. I started writing, and the connections got clearer as I went, and that post became the seed for one of our research papers. This is not uncommon, this is called freewriting. This is what happens when you give the machine a tape.

Writing is also the reason I remember anything. I refer back to my own blog constantly. Because I strained my brain writing those posts, rereading them re-fires the same neurons, and I reconstruct the understanding quickly. In this sense, the blog became my external memory. The thoughts I never wrote down do not stick well, because they were never fully thought.

If you think without writing, you only think you're thinking.

-- Leslie Lamport

 Writing in the age of LLMs

Is writing for thinking getting obsolete now since you can now argue anything with a model that has read everything?

Well, the model has read everything except what is in your brain! It knows the literature, the standard framing, and the consensus. But it does not know your half-formed intuition about why the standard framing may be wrong for this particular case. AI made a lot of progress, but I don't trust an LLM to take the creative leap and make a new connection. I think that would require another AI breakthrough. So, if you open the chat immediately on anything, you lose the opportunity to write/think for yourself.

This is a real problem, and it seems to be spreading quickly. We have been celebrating Amazon's six-pager as a great example of writing-for-thinking. Bezos had said: "There is no way to write a six-page, narratively structured memo and not have clear thinking." Unfortunately, with LLMs, that sentence has stopped being true. You can now produce six pages with no thinking at all, and the six pages still look like evidence that the thinking happened.

A model optimizing next-token probability cannot do your thinking. If you trust it to hold the pen, no thinking would get done. As everyone turns their thinking down and becomes a meat-proxy for generated text, if you still keep writing yourself, you would still be thinking for yourself. So writing is now a comparative advantage, and a widening one!

Anyways, enough about why you should write. Here is my advice on how you should write.

Rule 1: Mess up

The first rule of writing club is to produce in bulk with no restraints at all. Don't criticize, don't fix the typos, don't write in full sentences if you don't feel like it. The goal in this phase is to just accumulate text and get to a zeroth draft you can work with.

McPhee argues best for why getting anything down matters so much. Even if you had a bad writing session, it gave your mind something to work with. After you get something down, you can spot problems with it and think of better ways of phrasing things. But none of that happens without the drafted version to react against.

This is also how research papers get written. Open a notes.org file and treat it as a lab notebook: write while you do the work, explore every tangent, produce without any pressure to be presentable. In the Köroğlu post I compared this to the foal fattened in a pitch-black stable before any training begins. The key part of that frame is the stable. During this phase you guard the idea from critics, including and especially yourself. Ideas start out fragile and easily squished. So suppress judgment for a while and see what the thing becomes.

Rule 2: Tidy up

Now you must become the critic, the editor. Forget that you wrote this. Imagine some other guy wrote it, and do a harsh review. Cut ruthlessly. Take delight in deleting text the way you would in deleting code. If you cannot bear to delete a good sentence, move it to a junk buffer at the bottom of the file so you can tell yourself you might bring it back. Spoiler: you won't.

Don't be discouraged by how bad the first draft was. McPhee says the way to do a piece of writing is three or four times over, never once. This is good news. Thinking in multiple drafts takes the pressure off: you don't have to be spontaneous, brilliant on the first pass, or finished today.

I think the reason writing works so well for thinking is that it slows you down while keeping you on the problem. In that extra time, the insights and connections get room to surface. Chunking/abstracting happens in the background. Editing is then the magic trick where you pretend you had an organized thought all along. It is the packaging of the product.

Rule 3: Keep it simple, plain, and succinct

I am an Elements of Style guy. Strunk and White got it right, and their writing still reads fresh decades later. I adore Vonnegut too. His writing is simple as fuck and completely eloquent. It took a lot of balls to write that plainly. Complexity in prose is usually a place to hide sloppy thinking, or a way to weasel out of taking a stance. If you can't say it plainly, you probably haven't thought it through yet. And the way you think it through is by writing/editing.

Rule 4: Write without expectations

Write for yourself. The audience I have in mind is me. If others read it, that is a bonus, but the motivation has to be intrinsic, because the external rewards are far too delayed and too random to steer on. Writing like no one is watching also frees you up, and you can decide afterwards how much to share. Get your dopamine hit from the writing itself, not from people reading or sharing what you wrote, as that is very unreliable.

I have been writing and sharing on this blog since 2011, and around 2016 I started running into people at conferences who read it. I assumed it was a fluke, but it kept happening. Writing with a human voice turns out to get a lot of attention, and I am still surprised by how much. Paradoxically, you seem to get an audience only if you weren't doing it for the audience.

Rule 5: Put it on the schedule

You should stop trying to get inspiration to write and start scheduling it. Waiting for inspiration doesn't work, instead, putting your butt on seat and writing breeds good ideas for writing.

I find that keeping a posting schedule for the blog keeps me in "a writing frame of mind", which is really "a noticing frame of mind". Many weeks I tell myself a topic isn't interesting, but I start writing about it anyway, and then, what do you know, I am startled by the fount of interesting things that surfaces.

I also feel relieved after writing something as the thought is out of my system, I have closure on it, and I have room to think new thoughts. If a week goes by without a post, I feel clogged. So put writing on the calendar and keep it there until it no longer needs to be on the calendar.

entry.title: JIT bitmap text rendering for microcontrollers
entry.content:
JIT bitmap text rendering for microcontrollers Raph Levien, November 7, 2026

I've been working on vic-2350, a re-envisioning of an 80s home computer on an RP2350 microcontroller board. Of course, such a project needs text rendering. Though bitmap fonts are now out of favor, I chose them both for efficiency and because, at low resolutions, I prefer the aesthetic of a crisp, intentionally designed bitmap font over the blurry mush of antialiased font rendering. They still have a niche, if a narrow one.

I also wanted proportional spacing and kerning, again because I love the aesthetic of early Macintosh and its predecessors. Most text rendering in RP2350 projects is based on a fixed character cell, as achieving good performance is tricky.

This blog post presents a technique for extremely fast rendering of bitmap text on microcontrollers such as the RP2350. I've implemented it as part of my race-the-beam renderer, but the same technique would work when writing into a framebuffer as well. The core idea is a JIT to generate highly optimized code on the fly for rendering a string.

Racing the beam

Around the mid-80s, a split was happening in the way computers displayed text. The established technique was a fixed cell size, and hardware that looked up characters in a font ROM on the fly as the image was scanned out to the monitor. The advantage was very fast update and responsiveness with limited hardware. A lot of terminals worked this way, as did home computers. The downside was the lack of flexibility. In particular, only monospace fonts were supported.

The newer technique was a bitmap framebuffer, as pioneered on a line of computers originating with the Xerox Alto, continuing through the Apple Lisa, and finally becoming popular with the Macintosh. The framebuffer was vastly more flexible, but required a lot more computing power to keep updated. In the early 80s, you would generally watch text progressively render. I should also mention, graphics modes were generally available on home computers, but they were typically lower resolution than text mode and a 1MHz 6502 (or similar) was just not powerful enough, so serious text-based programs like word processors and spreadsheets used text mode.

Fast forward to the RP2350. It is capable of DVI video out with the help of the HSTX peripheral, but it is still entirely up to software to fill the video buffer. Some projects choose a framebuffer, but there's only 520kB of SRAM on the chip, so a framebuffer must be limited in either resolution or bit depth or both, and it would also be good for that RAM to be available to the app for other purposes. I've chosen instead to race the beam, filling a video buffer each scanline. That allows more visual richness and much lower latency, but is a hard performance constraint on the renderer. There's a budget of approximately 6 cycles per pixel. The lower we come in under budget, the more is available for rendering other graphical objects, and for other app functions.

Rust is not capable of meeting the performance requirement, so I started writing ARM assembly language. The renderer, and much of vic-2350, is now written in symbolasm, a programming language I've created for extremely high performance Cortex-M33 programming. Employing a JIT speeds up rendering further.

The rendering pipeline

Rendering is often modeled as a pipeline, and the vic-2350 renderer is no exception. The interface between application and renderer is a display list. At heart, that's just what it says, a list of display objects. The display list is double-buffered; one is being rendered and scanned out, and the other is built by the application. At each vsync, if the app is ready, the display list is swapped. Building the display list is not computationally intensive, but of course the app might be busy doing other things.

As the display list is of unknown size at compile time, it allocates. Display objects are packed into two vectors; one holds the display objects themselves, the other a list of indices into the first vector. A display object consists of a vtable, a bounding rectangle, and the object-specific payload. Allocation is acceptable because building the display list is not timing critical. Rendering is a different story. That said, it is important for the display list to be memory efficient, especially as there are two copies.

Before presenting, the indices are sorted into ascending y0 order.

During rendering, the renderer maintains an active list, which is just the subset of display objects that intersect the current scanline. At each scanline, objects for which y1 = y are deleted from the active list, and new objects with y0 = y are inserted, which is the reason for the sort earlier; it is exactly the order objects are inserted into the active list. The active list is kept in display object order.

Then the renderer just calls the render method for each display object in the active list. I'll do a bit more optimization soon, tracking opaque spans and eliding rendering work for spans of pixels that will be overwritten later, but that's not fundamental to the text rendering as presented here.

At the start and end of an object (when it's inserted and deleted) the renderer calls start and end methods on the display object. These methods can allocate scratch space and do other work to set up rendering of the object. There's a specialized bitmap allocator, which is both fast and deterministic.

Text display objects

All this gives us everything we need to implement text rendering as an instance of display objects.

The text object itself contains the string (1 byte per character), a pointer to the font, and foreground and background colors. RAM is precious, and more so for the display list because it's double buffered. In an earlier iteration of the renderer, I had an expanded version of the text stored in the display list, and that created unacceptable memory pressure when the screen was filled with text.

The start method allocates scratch space for both the JIT code and a 1 bit per pixel intermediate buffer, and invokes the JIT compiler, expanding the string into code.

The render method calls that code, which fills the 1 bit per pixel buffer, then runs a second pass to expand that 1 bit per pixel buffer into 16 bit per pixel RGB (565 format). This second pass runs at a sustained rate of 1.75 cycles per pixel.

The font is stored in extremely packed format. All the "ink" for glyphs is stored in a wide bitmap image, same height as the font. The packing also makes sure no glyph straddles a 32-pixel chunk boundary, so one row of font pixels can always be read with a single 32 bit load. If a glyph has space on either side of the glyph, that's not stored in the packed bitmap; rather, the space is in the per-glyph metadata.

In the spirit of micro-optimization, the packing algorithm also detects overlaps, as there's no requirement that pixels be unique to a single glyph. This optimization reduces the size of the font bitmap from 1140 to 960 bytes. Every byte counts, and more so as we add more fonts. The font bitmap needs to live in SRAM, as having it in flash could cause stalls during rendering at video rate.

I especially liked the {][} sequence (near the start of the second row). Any glyph contained within another glyph doesn't need to be packed separately. There are a few examples, some surprising. For example, l is the left side of U, and 0 is identical to () with the space between them removed.

The per-glyph metadata (not counting kerning) is conceptually four fields: the x position and width of the ink within the bitmap, the space on the left, and the advance. All this is tightly packed into a 32 bit integer.

JIT

In the generated JIT code, registers are assigned as follows:

r0 points to the beginning of the row of the packed font bitmap r1 is the output buffer, a one-line 1 bit per pixel image buffer r2 is the accumulator for the output bitmap r3 holds the bits of one glyph, extracted from r4 r4 holds 32 bits loaded from the glyph bitmap

In the simplest case, we add one glyph to the accumulator. The code looks like this:

ldr r4, [r0, #(x_offset / 32 * 4)] ubfx r3, r4, #(x_offset % 32), #(width) orr r2, r3, lsl #(x % 32)

There's additional code to output a word when it's finished (stmia r1!, {r2}), and to handle cases when a glyph straddles a 32 bit boundary. These are documented in text.sy. But there is one trick I do want to mention here: the code as above has a result-use delay between the ldr and ubfx (unsigned bit field extract). This is solved by shuffling the order of instructions somewhat: the last instruction for glyph i is reordered to follow the first instruction (ldr) of glyph i + 1, filling the delay slot, and reducing the cycle cost from 4 to 3.

Here's the inner loop of the code generator, focusing only on the case where the glyph doesn't straddle the accumulator. For each glyph, several values are packed into the g variable, then unpacked below: the offset within the packed font bitmap (which further breaks down into a bit offset and a word offset), the width of the inked part, the left side bearing, and the advance.

loop { g @r12 = *(glyphs + c * 4) // the next character, reading one past the end c = *text++ width @r7 = g[20..26] bit_offset @r4 = g & 31 if width == 0 goto blank // ubfx r3, r4, #offset % 32, #width ubfx_instr @r11 = *(ubfx_table + bit_offset * 4) // ldr r4, [r0, #offset / 32]; the font is narrower than 32 words, // so the offset fits, and strh leaves out what's above it. word_offset @r4 = g >> 5 ldr @r4 = ldr_base + (word_offset << 6) ubfx_instr += width << 16 *slot = ldr // left side bearing left @r4 = (g as i32)[16..20] *(code as *u32) = ubfx_instr // shift: where the glyph starts, relative to the word in r2. Branch is // also taken if negative. shift @r4 = pen + left room @r7 = 32 - width pen += g >> 26 #(shift - room) if #hi goto off_word // the delay: orr r2, r2, r3, lsl #shift d @r12 = *(orr_table + shift * 4) *((code + 6) as *u32) = d slot = code + 4 code += 10 #(n -= 1) if #ne goto loop }

Here's the corresponding machine code, ARM assembly code, and cycle count analysis from the symbolasm analysis tool:

134: f859 c028 1 ldr r12, [r9, r8, lsl #2] 136: f811 8b01 1 ldrb r8, [r1], #1 137: f3cc 5705 1 ubfx r7, r12, #20, #6 138: f00c 041f 1 and r4, r12, #31 139: b387 1/2 cbz r7, .Ljit_text.blank 141: f855 b024 1 ldr r11, [r5, r4, lsl #2] 144: ea4f 145c H 1 lsr r4, r12, #5 145: eb0a 1484 1 add r4, r10, r4, lsl #6 146: eb0b 4b07 1 add r11, r11, r7, lsl #16 147: 801c 1 strh r4, [r3] 149: f34c 4403 1 sbfx r4, r12, #16, #4 150: f8c0 b000 H 1 str r11, [r0] 153: 1934 1 adds r4, r6, r4 154: f1c7 0720 1 rsb r7, r7, #32 155: eb06 669c 1 add r6, r6, r12, lsr #26 156: 42bc 1 cmp r4, r7 157: d821 K 0/2 bhi .Ljit_text.off_word 159: f85e c024 1 ldr r12, [lr, r4, lsl #2] 160: f8c0 c006 1 str r12, [r0, #6] 161: 1d03 1 adds r3, r0, #4 162: 300a 1 adds r0, r0, #10 163: 3a01 1 subs r2, r2, #1 164: d1da K 0/2 bne .Ljit_text_0_loop loop 134-164: 23 cycles per iteration

The K flags indicate a possible delay in branches because the condition isn't known until the cycle before the branch. Here, 0/2 indicates 0 cycles if the branch is not taken, and 2 if it is. Neither of these can be optimized. The H flag indicates the instruction is 32 bits rather than 16 because of the use of "hi" registers (r8-r15). These are available in the LSP as well.

Performance

The basic loop is 23 cycles per glyph for the JIT plus 3 cycles times height for the bitmap generation. There's an additional cost of about 20 cycles for JIT and 2 cycles times height per 32 bits of output width.

This is astonishingly fast. The textdemo in vic-2350 takes about 21k cycles for the JIT and 42k cycles to run the JIT code. That adds up to about 2.6% of the available throughput of a single core of the RP2350. Expanding to 565 is actually about 3x more expensive. So it's fair to say it's as optimized as it can get.

While this was designed for race-the-beam rendering, it would work just as well writing into a framebuffer, especially a one bit per pixel framebuffer. Just generate the code, run it for each scanline.

It's tempting to cache the JIT output, but saving RAM is more important. The JIT output is about a 10x expansion over the input string. And, from the numbers above, it's clear that the cost of running the JIT is minimal.

The name "just in time" is apt; in the implementation in vic-2350, the JIT compiler runs under 100µs before scanout of the video line.

I wasn't able to find a direct performance comparison to an existing RP2350 text renderer. Probably the closest is dvhstx by Michael Bell and forked by Adafruit. That also ends up spending approximately 2-2.5 cycles total per pixel, but is limited to a 14x24 grid and also uses an RGB 222 mode, so its output bandwidth is only half as much (and this is where the lion's share of the time goes).

Dot Product Kerning

Kerning is a very important refinement for text rendering, otherwise the spacing looks irregular. The general mechanism in OpenType fonts is quite complex. For this project, I wanted something simple and efficient, so dusted off an idea that was originally motivated by trying to do text layout on GPU.

Basically, each glyph has two bitvectors, one each for the left and right side. To kern two glyphs, take the and of the right bitvector of the first glyph and the left bitvector of the second, then the popcount (number of 1 bits) of that, resulting in the number of pixels to kern. That's actually just the dot product of the two vectors, bits interpreted as 0 and 1. The kern tables require only two bytes per glyph, and kerning is super fast to evaluate.

Even so, kerning evaluation is done at display list build time, not racing the beam. When the kern is nonzero, a special negative space character is inserted into the string in the text display object.

For this font, I built the kerning table manually. Each bit is a specific feature, for example bit 0 represents the top right of the first glyph projecting out, and a corresponding lack of ink in the top left of the next glyph. So it is set on the right of T and Y, and also at the left of most lowercase letters and also A. It's not hard to imagine a tool that might help automate this, perhaps distilling kerning information prepared in other ways.

I haven't done a real implementation yet, but I suspect this idea might scale to real fonts: instead of bits and an integer kerning amount, the vectors would store continuous values (reasonably quantized). An additional nonlinear step after the multiplication but before the sum may also help. Dot products are of course ridiculously efficient to compute on GPU, while doing index chasing through OpenType tables is not. But that exploration is for another day.

Kerning improves quality considerably:

AI disclosure

This work is a refinement of the text rendering in pico-dvi-rs, which was hand-written. My draft of the JIT core was hand-written in Rust, then I used Claude to translate it to symbolasm and refine and optimize it. This blog is hand-written.

The symbolasm compiler and analysis tool is heavily LLM assisted, though it too evolved from an initial hand-written version.

I did a microtypography experiment that was a pretty cool result, but decided not to include it, partially because it would have increased the fraction of LLM content.

Like most other people in the industry, I struggle with the balance between quality and the acceleration that LLMs provide. Claude is exceedingly good at the low level tasks of coding; it easily found an edge case in my draft of the JIT compiler. I find that when used judiciously, LLM can improve quality, and I strive for that.

Related work

I wasn't able to find much precedent for JIT specifically for text rendering. Of course, there is a massive literature on JIT in general. On-the-fly code generation for bitblt was done for the Blit around 1982. See Bitmap Graphics SIGGRAPH 84 for more. An interesting detail is that they claim about 2500 characters per second; the raw performance of this on RP2350 hardware is almost 3 orders of magnitude greater, just counting the output to 1bpp (which is how the Blit's framebuffer was configured).

entry.title: Petered
entry.content:
Petered A Reading Note

The Peter Principle posits that people are promoted until they reach their level of incompetence. What happens after that point? The implicit assumption is that they stop getting promoted and linger at whatever level they’ve arrived at, and surely all of us can point to mediocre leaders who seem to exhibit exactly that circumstance. But in fact, that situation is not stable but subject to career pressure, as Christian Gläßel and Adam Scharpf define it in Making a Career in Dictatorship. Unable to move up, and very possibly unable to meet expectations, the person who is subject to the Peter Principle is at risk of losing their job, or even their entire career. Which means they might take an even greater risk to save it. Gläßel and Scharpf write:

The logic of career pressure also offers a compelling twist to the Peter Principle. The Principle posits that individuals in hierarchical organizations are promoted until they reach their level of incompetence, where they can no longer perform effectively and cease to advance. In contrast, our logic shows how these individuals may surpass this point and climb the hierarchy even further. Career-pressured individuals often take on high-risk, labor-intensive, or morally contentious tasks. By loyally executing the organization’s dirty work, they can reestablish their value, regain competitiveness, and even outpace peers who were previously ahead of them. Alternatively, they may resort to sabotaging superiors or higher-ups by making false allegations or revealing secrets to create vacancies above them and forcibly advance their careers.

Gläßel and Scharpf, Making a Career in Dictatorship, page 182

In other words, someone promoted up to their level of incompetence, sensing a threat to their own livelihood, becomes a threat to everyone else. I’m reminded here of David Graeber’s theory in Bullshit Jobs, that a great many management jobs are basically feudal retainers—people kept around in order to make the folks above them look good. Very often, making someone else look good may well mean tackling the dirty work for them so that they can keep their hands clean.

The petered leader has in effect been made an imposter—a real imposter, not a “syndromed” or perceived one. They must seem competent, to preserve the appearance that they belong in the role; while in fact they are not capable of delivering on their actual responsibilities and may have been quietly tasked with unrelated services both illegal and unethical. As a result, one of the primary tools of the real imposter is obscurity. Imposters cloak themselves in a fog of obfuscation and busyness, so that the people around them can never say for sure what it is they are doing, or how well (or not) they are doing it.

What we call imposter syndrome was originally termed imposter phenomena, a term that makes plain that it is something that can be observed, not merely felt. The transformation into a syndrome shifted the experience of being impostered by a patriarchal, white supremacist society into a medicalized disorder, something for which the impostered person must be treated. That’s a neat trick: to shift the locus of treatment to the mistreated person, rather than the system that caused her harm. But perhaps there’s even another, more diabolical move here. What if the popularity of imposter syndrome is, in part, a means of obscuring the actual imposters in our midst? What are we missing when we look inward instead of around?

entry.title: How to prove equations using diagrams, part 1
entry.content:
How to prove equations using diagrams, part 1

Initial functors

This post is cross-posted at the Topos Institute blog.

An e-graph, short for “equality graph,” is a data structure that maintains a congruence relation on expression trees: an equivalence relation stable under forming new expressions. First devised by Nelson and Oppen in 1980 (Nelson 1980; Nelson and Oppen 1980), e-graphs received a surge of new attention when Willsey et al demonstrated, via their software package egg, that e-graphs combined with equality saturation can be a fast, powerful, and adaptable tool for equational reasoning (Willsey et al. 2021). In my own work on CatColab, I’ve begun using egg’s successor, egglog (Zhang et al. 2023), to reason about finitely presented categories.

Standard presentations, beginning with Nelson’s PhD thesis (Nelson 1980), emphasize the data structures and algorithms needed to implement e-graphs, such as the union-find data structure. It’s crucial that work in computer algebra ultimately touch the ground in this way. Still, I can’t help but wonder what, abstracted from the implementation details, is really going on with e-graphs. The diagrammatic and visual nature of e-graphs, so apparent in the interactive egglog demo, will suggest to any category theorist that categorical ideas may be implicitly at work.

Two groups have recently proposed categorical semantics for e-graphs (Biondo, Castelnovo, and Gadducci 2025; Tiurin et al. 2025). Without going into specifics, both define an “e-hypergraph” to be a labeled hypergraph equipped with extra structure that, directly or indirectly, specifies an equivalence relation. Their starting point is to say what an e-graph is. Though I’ll eventually propose my own definition of an “e-diagram,” I will start by considering how e-graphs are manipulated, with the ultimate aim being to give a categorical and operational semantics for e-graph computation. The key concept will be that of an initial functor.

In this post, I’ll introduce the main ideas for categories without any additional structure. In comparison with e-graphs, this setting will be quite restrictive—it will correspond to allowing only unary function symbols—but it has the advantage of bringing us to the point with a minimum of setup. In future posts, we’ll generalize to categories with finite products and recover the standard setting of e-graphs.

Representing equations using diagrams

If you’ve encountered any abstract algebra, you’ve likely seen how category theorists represent equations between morphisms by drawing commutative diagrams. For example, saying that a square of morphisms

in some category commutes means that the equation \(g \circ f = k \circ h\) holds.

Let’s recall the formal definitions, which are standard if not without fine distinctions.

Definition 1 A diagram in a category \(\mathsf{C}\) is a functor \(D: \mathsf{J} \to \mathsf{C}\) whose domain \(\mathsf{J}\), the indexing category or shape of the diagram, is a small category. Further terminology:

the diagram is free if its shape is a free category, i.e., \(\mathsf{J} = \mathrm{Path}(G)\) is freely generated by a (possibly infinite) graph \(G\); the diagram is finitely presented if its shape is a finitely presented category; the diagram commutes, or is commutative, if for every pair of morphisms in \(\mathsf{J}\) with the same domain and codomain, their images in \(\mathsf{C}\) are equal.

Note that a diagram may well be both free and commutative: freeness is a property solely of the diagram’s shape, whereas commutativity also crucially concerns the diagram’s image in the target category.

In practice, we work with diagrams that are free and finitely presented. That means that the diagram’s shape is freely generated by a finite graph, a data structure easily implemented on a computer. When doing computer algebra, the target category will itself be finitely presented by generators and relations. Initially, the only equations that we “know” are the ones explicitly given as relations. Our aim is to derive further equations in the target category by manipulating diagrams in it.

But wait: if a diagram in a finitely presented category can be described using only graph-theoretic concepts, familiar to any computer scientist, what is the point of introducing categories and functors? We’ll see that category theory is indispensable to concisely describe the valid manipulations of diagrams. These manipulations take the form of morphisms between diagrams, which are functors satisfying an extra property.

Initial functors

Reasoning with diagrams, or “diagram chasing,”1 is the art of transforming a given diagram, say \(D: \mathsf{J} \to \mathsf{C}\), into another diagram \(D': \mathsf{J}' \to \mathsf{C}\), following certain rules of inference. In ordinary mathematical practice, nobody bothers to say what these rules are. We aim to be more systematic.

Let’s consider the obvious moves we could make. Given a diagram \(D: \mathsf{J} \to \mathsf{C}\), we could pull it back along a functor \(R: \mathsf{J}' \to \mathsf{J}\) to obtain another diagram \(D' \mathrel{\vcenter{:}}=D \circ R: \mathsf{J}' \to \mathsf{C}\). Conversely, we could extend the diagram \(D\) by finding a functor \(R: \mathsf{J} \to \mathsf{J}'\) along with a diagram \(D': \mathsf{J}' \to \mathsf{C}\) such that \(D = D' \circ R\):

Without assuming more, neither contemplated rule of inference is valid in the sense (to be made precise) of exactly preserving solutions to the equations presented by diagrams. For that, we need \(R\) to be a special kind of functor, an initial functor, characterized by the following definition/theorem.

Definition

Theorem 1 (Initial functors) A functor \(R: \mathsf{J} \to \mathsf{K}\) is initial, here denoted \(R: \mathsf{J} \twoheadrightarrow\mathsf{K}\), if any of the following equivalent conditions holds:

Pullback along \(R\) preserves limits: if \(\mathsf{C}\) is a category and \(D: \mathsf{K} \to \mathsf{C}\) is a diagram in \(\mathsf{C}\), then the canonical morphism between limits \[\lim_{\mathsf{K}} D \to \lim_{\mathsf{J}} (D \circ R)\] is an isomorphism, whenever the limits in question exist. Pullback along \(R\) preserves limits of sets: if \(D: \mathsf{K} \to \mathsf{Set}\) is a diagram of sets, then the canonical function between limits \[\lim_{\mathsf{K}} D \to \lim_{\mathsf{J}} (D \circ R)\] is a bijection. Slices relative to \(R\) are connected: for any object \(k \in \mathsf{K}\), the comma category \(R/k\) is non-empty and connected.2

For a proof of (the dual of) this equivalence, see (Riehl 2014, Lemma 8.3.4).

With a good intuition for limits, the limit characterization of initiality is useful because you can often see at a glance whether a given functor is initial just by imagining what will happen to a limit of sets. On the other hand, the slice characterization is useful in being concrete and syntactical. Recall that, given a functor \(R: \mathsf{J} \to \mathsf{K}\) and an object \(k \in \mathsf{K}\), the comma category \(R/k\) has

as objects, an object \(j \in \mathsf{J}\) together with a morphism \(f: R(j) \to k\) in \(\mathsf{K}\); as morphisms \((j, f) \to (j', f')\), morphisms \(h: j \to j'\) in \(\mathsf{J}\) making the triangle commute:

In the typical case that the categories involved are free and finitely generated, proving initiality—checking that each comma category \(R/k\) is non-empty and connected—thus reduces to a combinatorial problem.

Interpretation

Why are initial functors relevant to equational reasoning? In general, a limit of a diagram can be thought of as an object representing all possible solutions to the equations postulated by the diagram. This interpretation is clear in the ur-category \(\mathsf{Set}\), where a general formula gives the limit of a diagram of sets as the subset of all tuples of elements satisfying equations indexed by the shape’s morphisms. Namely, a limit of a diagram \(D: \mathsf{J} \to \mathsf{Set}\) is the set of all tuples \((x_j)_{j \in \mathsf{J}}\), where \(x_j \in D(j)\), such that all of the equations

\[ D(f)(x_i) = x_j, \qquad \forall f: i \to j\ \text{in}\ \mathsf{J}, \]

hold (Leinster 2014, Example 5.1.22). So, as pullback along an initial functor preserves limits, the initial functors are intuitively those that preserve the “solution set” of the system of equations presented by a diagram.

However, our interest lies in diagrams \(D: \mathsf{J} \to \mathsf{C}\) whose target is a finitely presented category \(\mathsf{C}\). Such categories rarely have many nontrivial products or equalizers. We can circumvent this problem in two ways.

First, we can always consider set-theoretic interpretations of the presentation, namely functors \(F: \mathsf{C} \to \mathsf{Set}\). Then the composite \(F \circ D: \mathsf{J} \to \mathsf{Set}\) is a diagram of sets and we are returned to the standard setting where all limits exist. This viewpoint is taken in the e-graph community when they speak of “uninterpreted functions” or “function symbols” (for us, generating morphisms of \(\mathsf{C}\)). Any equation deduced for uninterpreted functions remains true in any interpretation of them by actual functions between sets. Thus, if you have a formal system of proofs that is complete for equational reasoning with functions, then there exist proofs in that system for equations deduced using initial functors.3

Taking a little extra care, we can go further to deduce equations that hold in an arbitrary category \(\mathsf{C}\). Suppose we start with a singleton diagram in \(\mathsf{C}\), indexing a single object \(X \in \mathsf{C}\). The limit of that diagram exists trivially, being \(X\) itself. Thus, any diagram obtained by pulling back or extending the diagram along an initial functor will continue to have \(X\) as its limit. In particular, any two parallel paths in such a diagram originating at \(X\) must commute. We will use this technique in the calculations that follow. It will become more powerful when we extend to categories with finite products, since we can then start with any finite discrete diagram, the indexing objects of which act as “free variables.”

Examples and calculations

The remainder of the post will illustrate the concept of initial functor through commonly occurring examples and explicit calculations. The aim is to suggest how initial functors can be deployed for mechanical reasoning with diagrams, deferring to next time a further theoretical development.

Motifs among initial functors

Let’s begin with a few minimal examples of initial functors, acting as motifs or patterns. Each such example will give rise to a rule of inference for diagrammatic reasoning.

The target category \(\mathsf{C}\) for the diagrams is fixed throughout. That is, any initial functor should also be a morphism in the category of diagrams in \(\mathsf{C}\), the slice category \(\mathsf{Cat}/\mathsf{C}\).

Operation introduction: for any morphism \(f: X \to Y\) in \(\mathsf{C}\), the map of diagrams

is initial.

More generally, for any path \(X_0 \xrightarrow{f_1} X_1 \xrightarrow{f_2} \cdots \xrightarrow{f_n} X_n\) in \(\mathsf{C}\), the map of diagrams

is initial.

Congruence reduction: for any morphism \(f: X \to Y\) in \(\mathsf{C}\), the map of diagrams,4

sending both \(y\) and \(y'\) in the domain shape to \(y\) in the codomain shape, is initial.

Subsuming both operation introduction and congruence reduction, for any morphism \(f: X \to Y\) in \(\mathsf{C}\) and number \(n \geq 0\), the map of diagrams,

sending all of \(y_1,\dots,y_n\) to \(y\), is initial.

Equation introduction: suppose that the equation \(g \circ f = k \circ h\) holds in \(\mathsf{C}\), as depicted earlier. Then both maps in the span of free diagrams

are initial. More generally, this works for any path equation in \(\mathsf{C}\). As another example, we can introduce a nullary path equation, say \(\operatorname{id}_X = g \circ f\), as:

Later, we will formalize not just the rules but how to apply them, using ideas from category-theoretic rewriting. For the moment, we take for granted that when applying the rules in a larger context, the resulting functors are still initial. Or, you can check initiality by inspection in each application.

Pasting commutative squares

We’re ready to do our first calculation, proving the pasting law for commutative squares: that two commutative squares with a common edge can be juxtaposed to produce a commutative rectangle. The notation makes this seem obviously true—that’s what makes it good notation!—but it still needs a proof. We’ll present the proof in a highly mechanical style, where each diagram in the sequence is related to the previous one by an initial functor or, when introducing an equation, by a span of initial functors.

Assume: We are given the two commutative squares

By this we mean that the target category \(\mathsf{C}\) is generated by six objects, called \(X,X',Y,Y',Z,Z'\), and seven morphisms, called \(f,f',g,g',h,k,\ell\), subject to those two equations.

Construct: Start with the singleton diagram on \(X\), whose limit is trivially \(X\). Introduce the left- and right-hand sides of the path equation we want to prove:

Recognize the path \(X \xrightarrow{h} X' \xrightarrow{f'} Y'\) as the left-hand side of the first square, then introduce that equation:

Apply congruence reduction to the occurrences of \(f\):

Now recognize the path \(Y \xrightarrow{k} Y' \xrightarrow{g'} Z'\) as the left-hand side of the second square, then introduce that equation:

We’re already done, but we might as well tidy up by congruence reducing the occurrences of \(g\) and then \(\ell\):

Conclude: The outer rectangle commutes, since the limit of the diagram is still \(X\).

A monoid presentation

Consider a monoid with an element \(f\) satisfying the equations

\[ f^3 = \operatorname{id}= f^5. \]

That is, the target category \(\mathsf{C}\) is generated by a single object, say \(\bullet\), and an endomorphism, \(f: \bullet \to \bullet\), satisfying those two equations.

Start with the singleton diagram \(\{\bullet\}\) and introduce both defining equations, noting that since each equation has an identity on one side, they appear as cycles:

We leave the arrows unlabeled since every arrow lies over the generating morphism \(f\). We’ll now compute the congruence closure, iteratively applying congruence reduction until that is no longer possible. Arrows affected by a congruence reduction are colored the same on either side of the reduction, starting with the two blue arrows above. The first reduction is:

Next:

Congruence reducing three more times gives the sequence:

We could stop here, but we might as well reduce twice more, yielding the diagram that is the self-loop over \(f\). We have proved the equation

\[ f = \operatorname{id}, \]

since the limit of the diagram is the one we started with, namely the unique object \(\bullet\). In other words, the monoid presented is actually the trivial monoid. You might remember this as a special case of the fact in group theory that if a group element \(g\) satisfies \(g^m = \operatorname{id}= g^n\) for relatively prime numbers \(m\) and \(n\), then \(g = \operatorname{id}\).

Discussion

Category theory is often said to be abstract, even “abstract nonsense,” but it is the interplay between abstract and concrete that gives category theory its power. Initial functors, with their complementary intrinsic and syntactical descriptions, exemplify this interplay.

We’ve begun to explore how initial functors are the basis for an operational semantics for e-graphs. Rather than defining the individual steps and then chaining them together, as in the usual “small-step” operational semantics, we define the valid transformations invariantly via initial functors and then look for useful specializations. Beyond its conceptual content, this flexibility matters because practical systems tend to batch reductions together to improve efficiency. For us, that will often just amount to composing initial functors.

We haven’t yet made a direct connection with e-graphs, though there have been many hints. Another hint is that our final example is lifted directly from Nelson and Oppen’s early work (Nelson 1980; Nelson and Oppen 1980), where it is a running example. In future posts, we’ll tighten up the connection with e-graphs. We’ll also explain how the formalism generalizes to categories with finite products, the categorical counterpart to algebraic theories.

References Footnotes

In this series, we work first with bare categories and later generalize to cartesian categories. Diagram chasing in its most traditional form takes place in additive and abelian categories, a different direction of generalization. It would be fun to try to extend our methods to the additive setting, beginning with categories enriched in commutative monoids or abelian groups.↩︎

A category is connected if any two of its objects can be connected by a zig-zag of morphisms, i.e., there is an undirected path between them.↩︎

That is not to say that exhibiting a proof implied by completeness is easy or convenient. As I understand it, proof extraction is a topic of active work in the e-graph community.↩︎

When drawing a diagram \(D: \mathsf{J} \to \mathsf{C}\), the “type-theoretic” notation \(x: X\) names an object \(x\) in the indexing category \(\mathsf{J}\) that is mapped to the object \(X\) in the target category \(\mathsf{C}\). Thinking of the diagram as a term graph, the object \(x\) is indeed a “term of type \(X\).”↩︎

entry.title: I'm not a fan of Deno's security model (2024)
entry.content:
Iâm not a fan of Denoâs security model

this has been bothering me for a while now, so I want to write down my thoughts so I can get it out of my head and move on. weâre gonna talk about how Deno approaches security, specifically with its permissions system, and why I think this approach is fundamentally insecure and misleading.

wait, whatâs Deno?

Deno is a language runtime for JavaScript. it consists of a standard library, a package manager, a TypeScript transpiler and a bunch of other stuff thatâs not important for our story. itâs not a JavaScript implementation, so it does not interpret or compile JavaScript, it reuses V8 for that.

one of the flagship features of Deno is its permission system (itâs under the âSecure by defaultâ header on their landing page). the idea is simple: as JS code running in Deno needs the standard library to access the outside world, Deno can choose which accesses it allows or disallows, so when you run

shell deno run --allow-read=/tmp/dir --allow-run=uname code.ts

the standard library will only allow code.ts to read /tmp/dir and run uname.

additionally, a program can request permissions at runtime, so code like

typescript const r = { name: "read", path: "/tmp/dir" } as const; await Deno.permissions.request(r);

will display a nice little prompt in the terminal:

â â ï¸ Deno requests read access to "/tmp/dir". â Requested by `Deno.permissions.request()` API. â Run again with --allow-read to bypass this prompt. â Allow? [y/n/A] (y = yes, allow; n = no, deny; A = allow all read permissions) >

and you can grant or refuse it.

(aside: I really miss this feature in browser extensions. currently, if your extension needs potential access to any website, it needs to request actual access to all the websites, which is less than ideal)

if you like puzzles, this is the point where you can stop and think about what could go wrong with this system.

the prompts problem

of the two specific issues I want to point out this is the less severe one. weâll discuss it first because this was the first thing I noticed and it kinda immediately irked me when I first read about this.

(if youâre only interested in the more juicy part, you can skip to the next section).

so, this nice little prompt is displayed in the terminal. itâs not, like, a PolKit GUI window or anything, itâs just text on stdout waiting for input from stdin. this is a wild thing to do.

you see, terminal has a somewhat weird API. most of the commands / requests application can send to the terminal are sent in-band, by printing them to stdout. terminal can then reply by sending data to stdin. as Deno allows programs to print arbitrary data to stdout and read from stdin without requiring any permissions or doing any filtering, malicious code can send arbitrary commands to the terminal. itâs usually okay, because terminals wonât, like, execute shell commands just because stdout told them to, youâre supposed to be able to freely cat files without risking arbitrary code execution. itâs markedly less okay if you allow malicious code to do whatever with the terminal and then print a prompt on the same exact terminal.

you could, like, hide the prompt by messing with terminal colors. (this one got closed in 2026 because the permission prompt is âpartially visibleâ (you can see an emoji) and âAI agents tend toâ change terminal colors, so thatâs a âvalid use-caseâ)

or trick the user into pre-feeding approval into stdin.

or trick the terminal into feeding approval into stdin as a response to some request. (terminal wonât ever send Enter to stdin to avoid executing commands, but âpress Enter to continueâ is common enough to not be suspicious; the user never sees the actual prompt). hereâs an asciicast of that, I think it looks quite cool.

the specific issue on the screencast is long patched; the issue with terminal colors is not. that doesnât really matter because the real issue is using an attacker-controlled channel for security-sensitive information. itâs like executing attacker-controlled JS code on a webpage and then asking for password on the same page. you canât know that the page is in a safe state, so you canât trust any input.

even if Deno manages to patch every single issue with the âstandardâ escape codes, you never know which non-standard codes even exist out there. many terminals have some, itâs impossible to predict how they will interact with your prompt.

(aside: how come sudo can do it then? the difference is that sudo asks for the password first, before running any other code. to trick sudo that way youâd need to fuck up terminal state before you even type sudo, and do it quietly enough that you donât notice it while you type it. if some terminal allows it, Iâd consider it a bug in the terminal)

the --allow-run problem

so, thereâs a weird thing with this command I wrote above (Iâll copy it here for reference):

shell deno run --allow-read=/tmp/dir --allow-run=uname code.ts

what does --allow-run=uname even mean? itâs not like programs have canonical names, itâs not org.gnu.coreutils.uname, itâs not even /nix/store/8k1dmzr3gwzqdgw45nzj76902ca7g1is-coreutils-full-9.5/bin/uname. itâs just a shortcut for âlook at all the directories in PATH one-by-one to see if you can find uname thereâ.

you can set environment variables for the child process without needing any extra permissions, so what if we just

$ cat t.ts const command = new Deno.Command("uname", { // my current working directory, can be anything env: { 'PATH': '/tmp/tmp.7ofmKaNW83' }, }); const { code, stdout, stderr } = command.outputSync(); console.log(new TextDecoder().decode(stdout)); $ cat uname #!/bin/sh printf lol $ deno run --allow-run=uname t.ts lol

yeah.

once again, we have a pretty and convenient interface that doesnât really make sense from the security standpoint. it would be nice if programs were uniquely identified by their names, but theyâre not, and pretending they are leads to security holes.

funnily enough, I didnât even think that this issue would be there when I poked at Deno for the first time, so I havenât reported it until now (spoiler alert: this is a comment on a GitHub issue that I created for the problem Iâll explain below).

so letâs imagine we fixed that. itâs not that hard, we can force PATH to be whatever it was when the runtime started, or always require fully-qualified paths, or prompt with a fully-qualified path before running. are we safe now?

lol no of course weâre not. while PATH decides which executable gets run, dynamically-linked executables (so, like, most executables) require dynamic loader to actually start. dynamic loader is a program that, well, loads the executable into memory, finds its dependencies and does a bunch of other fun stuff we wonât get into. the important part is that dynamic loader is configurable via environment variables. you can probably see where this is going now.

LD_PRELOAD instructs the dynamic loader to load specific dynamic library when loading executables. dynamic libraries can execute arbitrary code on load. we can just pass LD_PRELOAD and weâve completely escaped the sandbox once again:

$ cat t.c #include <stdio.h> // ask dynamic loader to run this function on load time pretty please __attribute__((constructor)) void lol() { puts("lol"); } $ cat t.ts const command = new Deno.Command("uname", { // ask dynamic loader to load our evil library env: { 'LD_PRELOAD': '/tmp/tmp.7ofmKaNW83/liblol.so' }, }); const { code, stdout, stderr } = command.outputSync(); console.log(new TextDecoder().decode(stdout)); $ gcc -fPIC -shared t.c -o liblol.so $ # that's the real uname now! $ deno run --allow-run=uname t.ts lol Linux

I reported this some time ago and now they patched it by disallowing to set environment variables starting with LD_. this, once again, fixes a specific issue while ignoring the larger problem: âpermission to run a single commandâ is mostly not a useful concept. (you can do secure interfaces by allowing to run a single command, like git-over-SSH does, but generally both the environment and the command need to be prepared to handle it)

say, for example, our script wants to invoke the $EDITOR so user can edit some data (think git commit messages). thatâs a very natural permission request, and itâs also an unmitigated disaster because most editors are configurable enough for running one to be a full sandbox escape. itâs easy for user to absent-mindedly grant --allow-run=vim (âwell, sure, I want to edit this file!â), but then the script can just set VIMINIT='!rm -rf /*' and oops, all my files are gone. most programs are configurable, often in some ways you wonât think about (like LD_PRELOAD), and attacker controls the execution enviornment. âpatch some specific ways to configure programsâ is not the solution, the solution is to sandbox all the code, not just JS code.

when we discussed all this stuff in GitHub issues, a Deno developer wrote:

The main thing it protects you against is malicious code that isn't smart enough.

upon reading this, I was enlightened.

conclusions

deno tries really hard to do what the operating system should be doing. it emulates syscall filtering by filtering standard library calls. unfortunately, this breaks down the second you need to run code that doesnât use Deno standard library. it also uses somewhat flawed approach to permission management that looks good (wow, runtime prompts! omg, I can just --allow-run=uname!), but introduces security risks. in doing this, it implicitly requires user to understand all the implications of various permissions and their combinations, which can be really hard.

Deno process is not actually sandboxed, it only pretends it is. I didnât mention some more boring issues like âDeno doesnât prevent you from following symlinks that lead outside of the sandboxâ because they all just boil down to this simple one: the process is not sandboxed.

one can argue that this pseudo-sandboxing is better than nothing: after all, not all the malicious code is smart enough. I disagree: Deno permissions give a false sense of security and can lure someone into running untrusted code without proper sandboxing.

itâs possible that you can use Deno sandboxing safely if you:

never use more dangerous permissions like --allow-run, even with =cmd, that includes --allow-env, even --allow-env=VAR, for setting environment variables is memory unsafe and can affect libc functions, preferrably run with --no-prompt so your terminal canât be tricked, are careful about symlinks in directories you --allow-{read,write} to, are not concerned with resource exhaustion: thereâre zero permissions required to burn CPU or allocate memory.

in particular, you may be safe if youâre running untrusted code with no permissions at all in a non-interactive context and use some other mechanism to control resource consumption.

I still donât think you should do it. this path is riddled with footguns because youâre executing untrusted code in a fully-privileged process, and the moment you need some OS interactions youâre no longer running code âwith no permissions at allâ. you should not try to figure out which stdlib APIs can lead to a sandbox escape when combined. you should just use a proper sandbox.

Iâm not a fan of Denoâs security model.

so what do we do?

just bwrap untrusted shit.

also, please: donât harass Deno developers. we have a technical disagreement, but no technical disagreement was ever solved by harassment. this post is explicitly not an invitation to do it. Iâve already explained my point of view to them, they disagreed, and thatâs okay. you donât need to reiterate it, it wonât help anybody.

entry.title: A field guide to CAPTCHA types and how they break

FuckCaptcha is an open reference for understanding CAPTCHA types, their context and the approaches documented around them. It is intended for education and authorized research, not for evading protections on services without permission.
